conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/name: The Swiss Kappel Wars and the Schmalkaldic War
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/relig: These were the first wars fought between Protestant and Catholic states, and confessional allegiance defined the alliances. In Switzerland Zwingli openly argued that Zurich must use force to open the Catholic cantons to the preaching of the gospel, and the Catholic cantons fought to defend the old faith. In Germany the Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance for the Augsburg Confession, and the Pope supplied troops and money to Charles V. Yet Charles carefully presented the Schmalkaldic War as the punishment of rebellious vassals, not a religious war, so that Lutheran princes such as Maurice of Saxony could fight on his side; and issues of imperial authority, princely ‘liberties’ and Habsburg power were inseparable from religion. Historians (Bruce Gordon, Thomas Brady, Joachim Whaley) therefore treat religion as a major, but not the sole, cause.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/sides: Zurich and the Protestant cantons and cities
The Five Catholic Cantons (Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug)
Emperor Charles V and his allies
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/summa: The first wars between Protestant and Catholic powers broke out in Switzerland, where Zurich's attempt to force the gospel on the Catholic inner cantons ended with Zwingli's death at Kappel in 1531, and in Germany, where Charles V crushed the Lutheran Schmalkaldic League at Mühlberg in 1547. Both wars ended not in religious unity but in compromise settlements — the Second Peace of Kappel and, after further conflict, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) — that let each state determine its own religion.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/story:
In Zurich Huldrych Zwingli's Reformation, launched with the public disputations of 1523, abolished the Mass in 1525. The Swiss Confederation was a loose league of thirteen cantons, and the issue of religion became explosive in the ‘common lordships’ that several cantons governed together, where the Protestant and Catholic cantons clashed over which faith should be preached. Zurich and Bern formed a Christian Civic Union (Christliches Burgrecht) with other Protestant towns from 1527–28; the five Catholic inner cantons replied in 1529 with a Christian Union with their old enemy, Habsburg Austria. When the canton of Schwyz burned the Zurich pastor Jacob Kaiser in May 1529, Zurich declared war.

The First Kappel War of June 1529 ended almost without bloodshed. The armies faced each other near Kappel, and according to a celebrated story the soldiers of both sides shared a ‘milk soup’ across the border, the Catholics providing the milk and the Zurichers the bread. Mediators arranged the First Land Peace (26 June 1529), which favoured Zurich: the Austrian alliance was dissolved and the common lordships could choose their faith by majority. Zwingli, who had urged a decisive war, was dissatisfied and continued to plan for a wider anti-Habsburg alliance; the failure of the Marburg Colloquy with Luther in October 1529 left Zurich without German Lutheran support.

In May 1531, against Zwingli's advice to strike directly, Zurich and Bern imposed a food blockade on the inner cantons. On 9 October the Catholic cantons declared war and advanced on Kappel. On 11 October a hastily gathered Zurich force of a few thousand was overwhelmed; about 500 Zurichers died, among them some two dozen pastors and Zwingli himself, who had gone out as chaplain and fighter. His body was quartered and burned by the victors as a heretic's. A Protestant counter-attack failed at the Gubel on the night of 23–24 October. The Second Land Peace (November 1531) let each canton decide its own religion but protected Catholicism in the common lordships, halting the Reformation's expansion in central Switzerland. Heinrich Bullinger succeeded Zwingli and steered the Zurich church away from military politics.

In Germany the Protestant estates presented the Augsburg Confession to Charles V in 1530 and, threatened with enforcement of the Edict of Worms, formed the Schmalkaldic League in February 1531 under Saxony and Hesse. Luther, who had long taught that Christians may not resist the emperor, accepted from 1530 the lawyers' argument that princes could resist unlawful imperial force. For fifteen years Charles was held back by wars with France and the Ottomans and by the need for Protestant help; the League expanded, Protestant colloquies with Catholics at Regensburg in 1541 nearly reached agreement on justification, and Duke Henry of Brunswick, a Catholic, was driven from his lands by the League in 1542.

After the Peace of Crépy with France (1544) and a truce with the Ottomans, Charles prepared for war. The Council of Trent opened in December 1545, Luther died in February 1546, and Pope Paul III promised troops and money. In July 1546 Charles placed John Frederick of Saxony and Philip of Hesse under the imperial ban as rebels, and secretly won over the Lutheran Duke Maurice of Saxony with the promise of John Frederick's electoral title. The League's armies failed to exploit their early advantage on the Danube; Maurice's invasion of electoral Saxony drew John Frederick home, and the southern German cities submitted over the winter. On 24 April 1547 Charles's army, crossing the Elbe by a ford, routed the Elector at Mühlberg and took him prisoner. Wittenberg capitulated in May, and Philip of Hesse, surrendering at Halle in June, was also imprisoned. Charles, the story goes, refused to have Luther's body exhumed, saying he made war on the living, not the dead.

Charles's victory proved hollow. His Augsburg Interim of 1548, a temporary religious settlement imposed on Protestants pending the council, provoked widespread resistance, with Magdeburg as its centre. In 1552 Maurice of Saxony changed sides, allied with Henry II of France, and drove the emperor in flight from Innsbruck. The Treaty of Passau (1552) freed the captive princes, and the Peace of Augsburg (1555) recognised the Lutheran confession alongside Catholicism, allowing each prince to determine the religion of his territory — the principle later summed up as cuius regio, eius religio. Calvinists and Anabaptists were excluded, and the settlement's ambiguities would contribute to the Thirty Years' War.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/nameO: Zwingli argued that a Christian magistrate was bound to defend and spread the true gospel, and that Zurich must use force to open the Catholic cantons to evangelical preaching; he rode to Kappel as chaplain with a sword. The Catholic cantons fought for the Mass and the saints and treated his body as a heretic's. In Germany the Schmalkaldic League was formed to defend the Augsburg Confession, and Lutheran pamphlets portrayed the war as a defence of the gospel against the papal Antichrist. Pope Paul III issued a bull granting a crusading-style indulgence to those who joined the war against the heretics and sent papal troops under Ottavio Farnese, though Charles himself avoided calling it a religious war.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/relig: Zwingli's conviction that the magistrate must establish true worship, and Zurich's determination to protect evangelical preaching in the common lordships.
The Catholic cantons' resolve to defend traditional faith, demonstrated by the burning of Jacob Kaiser in 1529.
The Protestant estates' refusal to accept the Edict of Worms and the threat of its enforcement after the Diet of Augsburg (1530).
Charles V's sense of duty as emperor to restore the unity of the Church, and papal pressure to coerce the Protestants after the opening of the Council of Trent.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/other: Rivalry between Zurich and the inner cantons for dominance within the Swiss Confederation and over the shared common lordships.
The constitutional struggle in the Empire between Habsburg imperial authority and the ‘German liberties’ of the princes.
Maurice of Saxony's ambition to gain the electoral title from his cousin John Frederick.
Habsburg rivalry with France and the Ottoman threat, which determined when Charles could act.
The League's seizure of the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1542 and its expansion into ecclesiastical territories.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/trigg: The burning of Zurich pastor Jacob Kaiser by Schwyz in May 1529.
The Zurich and Bern food blockade of the Catholic cantons in 1531.
Charles V's imperial ban on the leaders of the Schmalkaldic League in July 1546.

Bern adopts the Reformation and joins Zurich's Christian Civic Union.

November: the Second Land Peace allows each canton its own faith.
The Nuremberg Standstill suspends action against the Protestants in return for help against the Ottomans.

Princes' Revolt under Maurice of Saxony; Treaty of Passau.

conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/casua: No overall estimate exists. About 500 Zurichers were killed at Kappel in 1531, according to Swiss chronicles, and several hundred more at the Gubel. The Schmalkaldic War involved few large battles; casualties at Mühlberg were in the low thousands, mainly on the Saxon side, and many more soldiers and civilians died of disease, plunder and siege in 1546–47 and in the Princes' Revolt of 1552, but no reliable figures have been established.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/effec: Switzerland was permanently divided into Protestant and Catholic cantons, with a balance that lasted until the Sonderbund War of 1847.
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) made religion a matter for each territorial ruler and gave Lutheranism legal recognition in the Empire.
Charles V's failure to restore unity contributed to his abdication and the division of the Habsburg inheritance between Spain and Austria.
Saxony's electoral title passed from the Ernestine to the Albertine line, reshaping German politics.
Zwingli's death discredited the alliance of reform with military power in Zurich, and Reformed leadership passed to Bullinger and later Calvin's Geneva.
The Interim crisis split Lutheranism between ‘Philippists’ willing to compromise and ‘Gnesio-Lutherans’ around Magdeburg, a conflict resolved only in the Formula of Concord (1577).
The Peace of Augsburg tied confession to territory, excluded Calvinists and Anabaptists and left their status to be fought over in the Thirty Years' War.
The failure of the Regensburg colloquy and the war confirmed that Catholic reform would proceed through the Council of Trent without the Protestants.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/legac: Kappel and Mühlberg showed that neither side could destroy the other by force. Out of military stalemate came the first legal frameworks for religious coexistence in Europe — territorial and limited, rather than personal toleration. Zwingli's death in battle remains a controversial part of his legacy, cited by Lutherans then as divine judgement and by historians now as the end of the ‘armed prophet’ model of reform.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/disse: In On Mending the Peace of the Church (1533) he urged both sides to accept moderate compromise on disputed matters rather than settle religion by force, as he had argued in his Complaint of Peace (1517).
The Venetian cardinal and the Strasbourg reformer led the Regensburg Colloquy of 1541, which agreed a formula on justification in an effort to reunite the churches without war.
The Anabaptists of Zurich and its neighbours refused to serve in Zurich's armies or to use the sword, and were persecuted by Zwingli's city for their refusal.
Until 1530 Luther insisted that Christians must suffer rather than resist the emperor by arms, and he warned Philip of Hesse against an aggressive Protestant alliance in 1528.
conflicts/kappel-schmalkaldic-wars/campa: The armies of the Five Catholic Cantons and of Zurich

The Catholic forces gathered at Zug and crossed into Zurich territory at Kappel on 11 October 1531, defeating the Zurich vanguard and killing Zwingli; a Protestant counter-thrust into Zug territory was routed by a night attack at the Gubel.
Charles V, the Duke of Alba and imperial, Spanish and papal troops

Charles gathered his army at Regensburg, withstood the League at Ingolstadt and followed its retreat along the Danube until the southern cities submitted; in spring 1547 he marched through Franconia and Bohemia into Saxony, forced the Elbe at Mühlberg and received Wittenberg's capitulation.
